_comment: Model catalogue. Data, not code, for three reasons: (1) model ids and pricing change faster than releases, (2) under IaC this becomes an SSM Parameter the CDK stack writes, so operators retune routing without a deploy, (3) adding a model is a config change a non-engineer can review. Verify ids with: aws bedrock list-foundation-models --region ap-southeast-2

models._disabled_reason: No qualifying scorecard on any task, and excluded on LATENCY rather than quality: p50 11.8s / p90 19.9s against the production 20s client timeout, with 9 of 98 plan calls over the ceiling (2026-08-28). It was `enabled` and second preference for generate_plan, so a Nova Pro outage failed over to a model already documented as unfit -- and because it declares both the quality and fast tiers, the cheapest-first fallback in route() made it a candidate for EVERY task. Re-enable only with a scorecard and a latency measurement under the ceiling.

_why_exclude.claude-haiku: 83.3% on repair across three identical reps, below the 90% floor. Perfect on defect repair and 71.4% on budget repair -- a structural weakness, not variance. It stays enabled and qualified for classify_intent (96.4%) and generate_plan (100%): `exclude` exists precisely so a model can be excellent at one task and barred from another, which `enabled: false` could never express.
_why_exclude.nova-pro: No repair scorecard, and it should not acquire one. It declares the fast tier so `available(tier)` would offer it as a cost-ordered fallback, but it is the quality-tier model -- routing repairs to it is a cost regression, not a quality win. Excluded as a routing decision, independent of any score.

scorecards._comment: Measured evidence, per model per task. A model is eligible for a task only with an entry here that meets the floor; see tests/test_multimodel.py, which fails the build if a routable model has no scorecard for a task it could serve. Recording the guardrail version matters: an intent score is a measurement of the classifier AND the policy in front of it, and version 2 unblocked cases version 1 refused.

generate_plan._source: evals/run_meal_plan.py, 11 cases, three clean reps each, paced

_unscored_tasks._comment: Tasks no eval measures, named rather than hidden. The test treats these as accepted gaps; deleting a task from here without adding a scorecard makes the build fail, which is the point.

generate_prose._note: Rule compliance, not literary merit. The node imposes a protocol -- placeholders only, no money, correct cheapest attribution -- and DEGRADES silently on any breach, dropping the sentence and shipping the bare table. So what is scored is whether a model can follow the protocol; a model that cannot produces a product with no prose in it and no error to show for it. Legacy 5.6 (subjective quality) stays open.

_measured_not_gated._comment: Measured, reported, and deliberately NOT used to gate routing, because the suite is too small for any threshold on it to mean anything. Distinct from _unscored_tasks, which is for tasks nothing measures at all. Expand the case set before gating.

repair_plan._status: GATED 2026-08-30. This entry is kept for the reasoning, not because it still applies. The suite was six cases and could not support a threshold; it was expanded to twelve, every case verified to discriminate against a model built to fail it, and re-measured over three reps per model. Nova Lite clears the 90% floor and serves repair; Claude Haiku does not and is excluded from this task only. See scorecards.repair_plan and routing.repair_plan.exclude.
repair_plan._option_kept_on_record: SPLIT THE TASK, if repair quality ever becomes the bottleneck. The two models are COMPLEMENTARY rather than ranked: Nova Lite scores 100% on budget repair and Claude Haiku 100% on defect repair. Routing `repair_budget` to one and `repair_defect` to the other would give 100% on both, where choosing either model alone gives up something. The graph already knows which kind of repair it is doing -- evals/run_repair.py separates them and src/prompts/ carries two distinct repair prompts, because a budget repair and a defect repair need different instructions. What it would cost: a second routing task, a scorecard per sub-task, and the qualification gate widening to cover both. Recorded here rather than built, because it is machinery for a problem that is not yet biting: a failed repair exhausts the bounded loop and produces an honest refusal, so the cost of the current arrangement is a refusal the shopper can act on rather than a wrong answer they cannot detect.

repair_plan._source: evals/run_repair.py, 12 cases (7 budget, 5 defect), guardrail version 2, live
repair_plan._reps: THREE reps each, and every rep identical. BedrockModelClient sets temperature 0.0, so these calls are near-deterministic: reps here confirm STABILITY rather than averaging out noise. The 18-point spread AGENTS.md warns about came from a different suite and configuration. Reps are still the right discipline -- they separate a stable number from a lucky one -- but on this suite they are cheap confirmation, not sampling.
repair_plan._finding: THE FAILURES ARE STRUCTURED AND OPPOSITE, not scattered. Nova Lite is perfect on budget repair and drops a defect repair; Claude Haiku is perfect on defect repair and drops two budget repairs. At six cases this looked like variance -- 'each failed a different case' -- and that reading was correct FOR THAT SUITE and wrong about the models. Twelve cases, three reps each, and the shape does not move.
